videos.summary: Free tier: 1,000 requests a day. Paid tier: 1 million a month. A per-second limit can't enforce that. This lesson explains throttling, rate limiting, load shedding and quotas, and how to build fair, billable API tiers.
chapters: 0:00 Are throttling, rate limits and quotas the same thing?

videos.title: API Authentication: API Keys vs JWT vs HMAC Signatures vs mTLS
videos.summary: A mobile app, a partner backend, a payment webhook and an internal service all call your API, and each must prove who it is. This lesson compares the five common authentication methods and where each one fits.
chapters: 0:00 API keys, JWT, signatures or mTLS: which one proves who you are?

videos.title: API Authorization & BOLA: Scopes, Ownership Checks and Where They Live
videos.summary: User 42 has a valid token, calls GET /orders/1001, then changes it to 1002 and reads someone else's order. Authentication worked; authorization didn't. This is BOLA, the #1 risk in the OWASP API Security Top 10.
chapters: 0:00 Your API knows who the user is. But does it check what they own?
1:45 The fix: check at the data access
2:19 Why not only at the gateway?

videos.title: API Gateway Explained: What Belongs in It, BFFs & Avoiding a SPOF
videos.summary: Twenty microservices, many clients, and every request needs TLS, authentication and rate limiting. Instead of rebuilding that 20 times, you put one front door in front: an API gateway. This lesson covers what it should do, what it must not do, and how to keep it from becoming a single point of failure.
chapters: 0:00 What belongs in an API gateway, and what does not?
2:41 Don't make it a single point of failure

videos.title: Retries, Exponential Backoff & Jitter: How Retries Cause Outages
videos.summary: A dependency returns 503 for two seconds. One retry would fix it, but a thousand clients retrying in lockstep can turn that blip into a 20-minute outage. This lesson shows how to retry safely.
chapters: 0:00 Why can a retry take down the service it was trying to reach?

videos.title: API Timeouts & Deadline Propagation: Budgets, gRPC & Cancellation
videos.summary: The gateway gives a request 2 seconds, but every service behind it waits 10. The user gives up while your backend keeps working on an answer nobody will see. This lesson shows how to pick timeout values and propagate deadlines through a call chain.
chapters: 0:00 How do you stop a slow call from eating your whole budget?
0:11 2 s at the edge, 10 s inside

videos.title: Webhooks: Reliable Delivery, HMAC Signing, Retries & Duplicate Handling
videos.summary: Instead of polling, your payment provider calls you: a webhook. Simple idea, but designing reliable webhook delivery (and a safe receiver) is a classic system design interview question.
chapters: 0:00 How do you deliver a webhook that never gets lost?

videos.title: Async APIs for Long Jobs: 202 Accepted, Job Status, Polling vs Callbacks
videos.summary: A 300-page PDF takes 10 minutes to parse, chunk, embed and index. You can't hold an HTTP request open that long. This lesson shows how to design async APIs for long-running work.
chapters: 0:00 What should an API do when a request takes ten minutes?
0:59 The job is a resource: an operation

videos.title: API Contracts & OpenAPI: Contract-First, Typed Clients & Pact
videos.summary: A backend engineer renames one field, every test passes, and the mobile app crashes for everyone. Nobody tested the contract. This lesson shows how OpenAPI specs, generated clients and contract tests catch breaking changes before release.
chapters: 0:00 How do two teams agree on an API before writing code?

videos.title: API Backward Compatibility: Breaking Changes & Expand-Contract
videos.summary: Five versions of your mobile app are in the wild, and some users never update. Every response must work for all of them. This lesson shows which API changes break clients, and how to evolve and remove fields safely.
chapters: 0:00 Which changes break clients, and which are safe?
0:11 Five app versions in the wild
2:10 Removing a field: expand and contract

videos.title: Relational Model & SQL Basics: Keys, Constraints, Join Types & Why SQL
videos.summary: "Revenue per product last month?" "Customers who never ordered?" With a relational database, each is one SQL query. This lesson covers the relational model and why SQL is still the default choice for most systems.
chapters: 0:00 Why is SQL still everywhere after fifty years?
2:28 When is relational the right default?

videos.title: Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, Anomalies & Junction Tables
videos.summary: One big users table with comma-separated roles and copied manager emails works, until a role is renamed and the data quietly drifts. This lesson explains normalization, the anomalies it prevents, and how to model relationships properly.
chapters: 0:00 Why does the same fact sometimes live in three places?

videos.title: Denormalization: Counter Caches, Materialized Views & Consistency
videos.summary: Counting 2 billion likes for every post on every feed load is far too slow. The fix is to store the answer: denormalization. This lesson covers when to denormalize, the forms it takes, what it costs, and how to keep the copies consistent.
chapters: 0:00 When is it right to break the normalization rules?

videos.title: B-Tree Indexes Explained: Fan-Out, Range Scans, Write Cost & UUIDv4 Keys
videos.summary: 100 million orders, and "my latest orders" loads by reading about four pages. That's the B-tree. This lesson explains how B+ tree indexes work, why they're fast, and what they cost.
chapters: 0:00 How does an index find one row among a billion?

videos.title: Composite, Covering & Partial Indexes: Column Order and Leftmost Prefix
videos.summary: A job queue with 50 million rows but only 300 pending, and a report filtering orders by status and date: each needs a different kind of index. This lesson covers composite, covering, partial and expression indexes.
chapters: 0:00 Does the order of columns in an index really matter?

videos.title: LSM Trees & SSTables: Memtable, Compaction, Bloom Filters vs B-Trees
videos.summary: A million IoT sensors, 100,000 writes per second, all day. A B-tree would drown in random page updates. Cassandra, RocksDB and ScyllaDB use a log-structured merge tree instead. This lesson explains how it works and how it compares with B-trees.
chapters: 0:00 How do databases like Cassandra write so fast?

videos.title: SQL Query Optimization: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Join Algorithms & N+1 Problem
videos.summary: Your order history page suddenly takes 8 seconds. Same code, more data. This lesson shows how to read query plans, why the optimizer picks what it picks, and how to find and fix the N+1 problem in an ORM.
chapters: 0:00 Your query is slow. Where do you even start?

videos.title: ACID Explained: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability & the WAL
videos.summary: Alice sends Bob $100. If the server crashes halfway, the money can't vanish or appear out of thin air. This lesson explains each letter of ACID, and how databases actually guarantee durability with a write-ahead log.
chapters: 0:00 What does a database really promise when it says transaction?

videos.title: Isolation Levels & Write Skew: Snapshot Isolation vs Serializable
videos.summary: Two doctors, one rule: at least one must stay on call. Both check, both go off call, both transactions succeed, and nobody is on call. Every row was updated correctly. This is write skew, and whether it can happen depends on your isolation level.
chapters: 0:00 Two transactions both passed the check. So why is the data wrong?

videos.title: MVCC Explained: Row Versions, Snapshots, xmin/xmax & VACUUM
videos.summary: A 20-minute analytics report runs on production Postgres while thousands of orders are written every second, and neither waits for the other. That's multi-version concurrency control. This lesson explains how it works and what it costs.
chapters: 0:00 How can readers and writers work on the same row at once?

videos.title: Database Locks & Deadlocks: Shared vs Exclusive, Lock Ordering
videos.summary: Two transfers run at once: A → B and B → A. Each locks its source account, then waits for the other's. Forever. This lesson explains database locks, how deadlocks form, and how to prevent them.
chapters: 0:00 Why do two transactions sometimes wait for each other forever?

videos.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking: Version Checks, FOR UPDATE
videos.summary: A flash sale: 100 pairs of sneakers, 10,000 shoppers clicking BUY at the same moment. Read the stock, subtract one, write it back, and you oversell. This lesson compares the three ways to stop lost updates: pessimistic locks, optimistic version checks, and atomic conditional updates.
chapters: 0:00 Should you lock the row or just check the version?

videos.title: NoSQL Explained: 4 Families, BASE vs ACID & When Not to Use It
videos.summary: User sessions in Postgres: 100,000 simple lookups per second, no joins, no reports, and the database is struggling. Should it move to NoSQL? This lesson explains why NoSQL exists, what you give up, and when a relational database is still the right call.
chapters: 0:00 When is NoSQL the wrong choice?

videos.title: Key-Value Stores Explained: Redis vs DynamoDB vs etcd
videos.summary: Every "add to cart" has to save the cart and read it back in milliseconds, for millions of shoppers. No joins, no reports, just "give me the cart for user 42". That's the perfect job for a key-value store.
chapters: 0:00 Redis, DynamoDB or etcd: what is each one really for?

videos.title: Document Databases Explained: Embed vs Reference, MongoDB Limits
videos.summary: A product catalog sells shoes, laptops and sofas, and every category has different attributes. In one relational table that's a hundred mostly empty columns. A document database stores each product as its own JSON document. This lesson covers how to model documents well, and where they break.
chapters: 0:00 Should you embed the data or reference it?

videos.title: Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra Table Design for a Chat App
videos.summary: A chat app stores billions of messages, and opening a channel must show the latest 50 instantly while millions of new messages are written every minute. Discord solved exactly this with a wide-column store. This lesson shows how to design the table.
chapters: 0:00 How do you design a Cassandra table for a chat app?

videos.title: Graph Databases Explained: Friend-of-Friend, Fraud Rings & Cypher
videos.summary: "People you may know": friends of your friends who aren't your friends yet. In SQL that's a self-join per hop, and at social-network scale it crawls. Graph databases are built for exactly this kind of query.
chapters: 0:00 How do you find friends of friends without a slow join?
2:34 When to choose a graph DB

videos.title: Time-Series Databases: Downsampling, Retention & Cardinality
videos.summary: 10,000 servers reporting CPU every minute is 14.4 million rows a day, and over 5 billion a year, for a single metric. Dashboards want the last hour instantly, and plain Postgres starts to groan. This lesson explains how time-series databases handle it.
chapters: 0:00 Why are metrics too heavy for a normal database?

videos.title: Leader-Follower Replication: Sync vs Async, Lag & Failover
videos.summary: A Postgres primary with two replicas. At 2:03 am the primary's disk dies. The last 200 ms of orders were confirmed to customers but never reached a replica, so when you promote one, those orders are gone. This lesson explains why, and how to prevent it.
chapters: 0:00 What happens to your data when the leader dies?

videos.title: Read Replicas & Replication Lag: Fixing Stale Reads After Writes
videos.summary: A user changes their display name, clicks save, and the page shows the old name. Nothing is broken: the write went to the primary, the read went to a replica half a second behind. This lesson shows how to scale reads with replicas without confusing your users.
chapters: 0:00 Why does a user not see the post they just wrote?

videos.title: Multi-Leader & Leaderless Replication: Conflicts, CRDTs, Quorums
videos.summary: A collaborative notes app with users in Europe and the US. With one leader in Virginia, every keystroke from Berlin crosses the Atlantic, and a Virginia outage stops all writes. What if both regions could accept writes? This lesson covers multi-leader and leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication.
chapters: 0:00 What if two people edit the same record in two continents?

videos.title: Database Sharding Fundamentals: Choosing a Shard Key & Pitfalls
videos.summary: A users table with 2 billion rows and 40 TB of data. The primary is on the biggest machine you can buy and its disks are at their write limit, and read replicas don't help because every replica must apply every write too. It's time to shard.
chapters: 0:00 When one database is not enough, how do you split it?

videos.title: Range vs Hash Partitioning: Scans, Hot Spots & Compound Keys
videos.summary: Two systems, both too big for one machine: a logging platform where engineers ask for the last hour of logs, and a user service that looks up one user by ID. Should they be partitioned the same way? No, and this lesson explains why.
chapters: 0:00 Range or hash: which way should you split the data?

videos.title: Rebalancing & Hot Partitions: Consistent Hashing and Key Salting
videos.summary: A celebrity with 50 million followers posts a photo. Millions of likes hit the same post ID on one partition: that shard is pinned at 100% CPU while the other 19 sit idle, and adding nodes won't help. This lesson covers how to rebalance data and how to fix hot keys.
chapters: 0:00 What do you do when one shard gets all the traffic?

videos.title: Secondary Indexes in Partitioned Data: Local vs Global (GSI)
videos.summary: Your orders table is partitioned by order_id across 50 partitions. Then the warehouse team asks for every order with status SHIPPED. Status isn't the partition key, so which partition do you ask? All fifty? This lesson explains the two ways to index it.
chapters: 0:00 How do you query by a column that is not the shard key?

videos.title: Postgres Table Partitioning: Pruning, Retention & No Sharding
videos.summary: An audit_log table with 3 billion rows, growing by 10 million a day. Queries for last week crawl, indexes don't fit in memory, and deleting old rows takes hours and bloats the table. You don't need more servers: you need to split this one table inside the same database.
chapters: 0:00 Can you handle a billion rows without sharding?

videos.title: Distributed ID Generation: Snowflake, UUID v7 vs UUID v4, ULID
videos.summary: Fifty instances of an order service take orders at the same time. Every order needs a unique ID right now, without asking a central database, and ideally newer orders should get bigger IDs. This lesson compares the ways to generate primary keys at scale.
chapters: 0:00 How do a thousand servers make unique IDs without talking?

videos.title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Expand-Contract & Backfills
videos.summary: You rename a column from name to full_name and deploy. During the rolling deploy, half your servers still run old code that reads name, and checkout breaks for ten minutes. This lesson shows how to change a production schema without downtime.
chapters: 0:00 How do you change a table that is serving live traffic?

videos.title: Database Connection Pooling: PgBouncer & Sizing Your Pools
videos.summary: Black Friday: your API autoscales to 200 pods, each with a pool of 20 database connections. That's 4,000 connections to a Postgres server configured for 500. Connections are refused, memory runs out and the database falls over, even though the queries are fast. This lesson explains connection pooling and how to fix it.
chapters: 0:00 Why does your database fall over with only a few hundred users?

videos.title: OLTP vs OLAP: Row vs Column Stores, Warehouses, ETL vs ELT
videos.summary: Every Monday at 9:00 the finance team runs its revenue report straight on the production database, scanning two years of orders, and every Monday at 9:00 checkout slows to a crawl. The report is fine; it's just running in the wrong place. This lesson explains OLTP vs OLAP and where analytics belongs.
chapters: 0:00 Why can't your production database run the analytics?
0:12 The Monday report that kills checkout
1:54 Why not analytics on the OLTP DB?

videos.title: Change Data Capture (CDC): Debezium, Kafka & the Dual-Write Problem
videos.summary: A product service saves a price change to Postgres, then updates Elasticsearch. One day the Elasticsearch call times out after the database commit, and search shows the old price forever. This lesson explains the dual-write problem and how change data capture fixes it.
chapters: 0:00 How do you update the database and Kafka without losing either?

videos.title: Distributed SQL Explained: Spanner, CockroachDB, Raft & TrueTime
videos.summary: A global payments ledger: every transfer must be a real ACID transaction, customers are on three continents, and a whole cloud region can fail without losing a committed transfer. One Postgres server can't do that, and hand-sharding is hard. This lesson explains NewSQL / distributed SQL and its trade-offs.
chapters: 0:00 Can a database be global, consistent and SQL?

videos.title: How to Choose a Database: Access Patterns & Polyglot Persistence
videos.summary: "Which database would you use?" Answering "MongoDB, because it scales" or "Postgres, because I like it" is a red flag in a system design interview. The right answer starts with questions about the data. This lesson gives you a repeatable way to choose.
chapters: 0:00 With so many databases, how do you pick one?
2:07 Every extra store has a cost

videos.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: Which Numbers to Ask First
videos.summary: "Design a URL shortener." Is it a hobby project with a thousand links, or a global service creating a hundred million links a day? The architecture is completely different, so the first step of any estimate is asking for the right numbers. This lesson starts the capacity estimation series.
chapters: 0:00 Which numbers should you ask for first in a design interview?

videos.title: Latency Numbers & Powers of Two Every Engineer Should Know
videos.summary: "We get one million requests a day. Is that a lot?" Experienced engineers answer in two seconds: about twelve requests per second, easy for one server. The trick is a handful of numbers you know by heart. This lesson covers them.
chapters: 0:00 What are the numbers every engineer should know by heart?
0:11 Is 1 million requests a day a lot?

videos.title: How to Estimate RPS: DAU, Reads vs Writes & Peak Traffic
videos.summary: "100 million daily active users, each reading their feed 10 times a day. How many requests per second?" Turning that sentence into a number in 30 seconds tells you whether you need one server or a thousand. This lesson shows the method.
chapters: 0:00 How many requests per second does your product really get?

videos.title: Peak vs Average Traffic: How to Survive a 50× Spike
videos.summary: A ticket sale opens at 10:00. On a normal day the site handles 2,000 requests per second; at 10:00 it's 100,000, fifty times more. If you sized for the average, the site is already down. This lesson explains peak factors, headroom, and how to absorb bursts.
chapters: 0:00 Can your system survive a fifty times spike?

videos.title: Read/Write Ratio: How 100:1 Reads Shape Your Architecture
videos.summary: A short link is created once and clicked a hundred times; a sensor reading is written every second and read maybe once a day. These systems have opposite shapes, and that one ratio should change almost every decision in your design.
chapters: 0:00 How does a hundred to one read ratio shape the design?

videos.title: Storage Estimation: Size × Count × Retention × Replicas
videos.summary: Users upload 500 million photos a day, each about 2 MB. How much storage over five years? The quick answer misses a factor of three or more: the difference between a sensible budget and a very unpleasant surprise.
chapters: 0:00 How much storage will you need in five years?

videos.title: Bandwidth Estimation: Ingress, Egress, Gbps & CDN Offload
videos.summary: 10,000 people watch at the same time, each stream at 5 Mbps. Can one data center link handle it, and what's the monthly bill? Bandwidth is often the most expensive line in a video platform's budget, so you need to estimate it.
chapters: 0:00 How many gigabits per second is your product?

videos.title: Cache Sizing: Working Set, the 80/20 Rule & Redis Nodes
videos.summary: A URL shortener serves a billion redirects a day and you want Redis in front of the database. How much memory: 10 GB or 1 TB? Too small and the hit rate collapses; too large and you pay for memory nobody uses. This lesson shows how to size a cache.
chapters: 0:00 How big should your cache be?
0:10 How much memory for the cache?

videos.title: How Many Servers Do You Need? Capacity, 60% Target & N+2
videos.summary: Your API must handle 12,000 requests per second at peak. How many servers or Kubernetes pods? Dividing by a number you heard somewhere isn't enough: you need per-instance capacity, a safe utilization target, and room for failures.
chapters: 0:00 How do you know how many servers to buy?

videos.title: Growth Projections: Compound Growth, Runway & When to Shard
videos.summary: Your database is at 40% CPU and traffic is growing fast. Will it survive next year? If you only notice at 100% you're months too late, because sharding takes a quarter or more. Growth projections tell you when to start.
chapters: 0:00 When will your database stop being enough?

videos.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: Full URL Shortener Drill
videos.summary: In an interview you have about five minutes for estimation, out loud, on a whiteboard. Let's practice the full drill end to end for a URL shortener: assumptions, traffic, peak, storage, bandwidth, cache and servers.
chapters: 0:00 Can you size a URL shortener in under five minutes?

videos.title: Architecture Diagrams: Sync vs Async, Read/Write Paths, C4
videos.summary: Estimates done, you pick up the marker, and five minutes later the whiteboard is a tangle of boxes and crossing arrows. A clear diagram is half of a system design interview. This lesson shows how to draw one properly.
chapters: 0:00 What should a good architecture diagram show?

videos.title: Identifying Bottlenecks: Find What Breaks First (50k Writes/s)
videos.summary: Your design handles 100,000 requests per second on paper, then launch day comes and everything crawls. Not because every part is too small, but because one part is. This lesson shows how to find the bottleneck before production does.
chapters: 0:00 At fifty thousand writes a second, what breaks first?
0:10 Fast on paper, slow on launch day

videos.title: Identifying SPOFs: Ask 'What If This Dies?' for Every Box
videos.summary: Twenty servers across three zones, fully redundant... until the login provider goes down and nobody can sign in. A single point of failure was hiding in a dependency nobody drew. This lesson shows a systematic way to find SPOFs in any design.

videos.title: Load Balancer Fundamentals: What It Does & How to Make It HA
videos.summary: One server can't keep up, so you add three more. Now who decides which one gets each request, and what happens when one crashes? Welcome to Phase 3: load balancers.
chapters: 0:00 Your app runs on ten servers. How do users reach all of them through one address?
2:44 Example: ALB in front of ECS

videos.title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing: NLB vs ALB, TLS Termination
videos.summary: One load balancer only sees addresses and ports; the other reads every HTTP request. Both are 'load balancers', but they work at different layers, and the wrong choice costs you speed or features.
chapters: 0:00 Your load balancer is layer 4 or layer 7. What can each one actually see?

videos.title: Round Robin vs Weighted Round Robin: When Taking Turns Fails
videos.summary: The simplest way to share work is to take turns. Round robin is the default in many load balancers, and it works well until your servers or your requests aren't equal.
chapters: 0:00 One server is twice as big as the others. Should it get the same traffic?

videos.title: Least Connections, EWMA & Power of Two Choices Explained
videos.summary: Your servers stream LLM answers: some finish in two seconds, others take a minute. Round robin piles long streams onto one server. You need a balancer that looks at actual load.
chapters: 0:00 Round robin sends a request to a server that is already drowning. Why?

videos.title: Consistent Hashing Explained: Hash Ring, Virtual Nodes, Rendezvous
videos.summary: Spread cache keys with hash(key) % 4 and it works, until you add a fifth server and about 80% of keys move. Consistent hashing fixes exactly this.
chapters: 0:00 You add one cache server, and almost every key moves. How do you stop that?

videos.title: Sticky Sessions & IP Hash: Why Session Affinity Bites
videos.summary: A user adds three items to their cart, the next request hits another server, and the cart is empty. The quick fix is a sticky session. It works, but it comes with a bill.
chapters: 0:00 A user's cart is empty after a refresh. What went wrong?

videos.title: Health Checks: Liveness vs Readiness & Why Deep Checks Are Dangerous
videos.summary: A server answers pings but fails every real request, and the load balancer keeps sending it traffic. Or one database hiccup marks every server unhealthy at once. Health checks decide who gets traffic, so getting them right matters.
chapters: 0:00 One bad health check pulls every server out of the pool. How?

videos.title: Service Discovery: Client-Side vs Server-Side, DNS & Kubernetes
videos.summary: Your order service needs to call payments, but payments runs as twelve containers whose IPs change on every deploy. Hard-coding addresses is impossible. Services need a way to find each other.
chapters: 0:00 Container addresses change every minute. How do services find each other?

videos.title: Reverse Proxy Config in Production: Timeouts, Retries, Buffering
videos.summary: You put NGINX in front of your API, keep the defaults, and ship. Then a slow client ties up workers, a dead backend makes requests hang for a minute, and a retry storm takes everything down. A reverse proxy is only as good as its configuration.
chapters: 0:00 Your proxy runs on default settings. What breaks first in production?

videos.title: Load Shedding & Traffic Shaping: Survive Overload (Black Friday)
videos.summary: Black Friday: five times the normal traffic, and everything slows down together until nothing works. The counterintuitive fix is to reject some requests on purpose so the important ones survive.
chapters: 0:00 Traffic doubles. Is it better to fail everyone, or reject some on purpose?

videos.title: Global Server Load Balancing: GSLB, Anycast & Regional Failover
videos.summary: Your app runs in one region: users far away wait 200 ms per round trip, and one outage takes everyone offline. With several regions, how does each user reach the right one, and what happens when one goes dark?
chapters: 0:00 A user in Mumbai, servers in Virginia. How do you send them somewhere closer?

videos.title: Failover Strategies: Active-Active vs Active-Passive, Hot/Warm/Cold
videos.summary: 3 AM, your primary region goes down. Do you have a second region already serving, an idle standby, or just backups and a runbook? That decides whether you're down for seconds, minutes, or hours.
chapters: 0:00 Three in the morning, the primary dies. What takes over, and how fast?

videos.title: Blue-Green Deployments & Canary Releases with Weighted Traffic
videos.summary: What if a new version got only 5% of traffic first, you watched the numbers, and you could switch back in seconds? Load balancers make that easy with blue-green deployments and weighted traffic splitting.
chapters: 0:00 How do you ship a release without every customer finding the bug?

videos.title: Autoscaling Explained: Which Metric? (CPU vs RPS vs Queue Depth)
videos.summary: Your API needs four servers at night and forty at lunch. Autoscaling adds and removes capacity as demand changes, but scale on the wrong signal, or too slowly, and it can't save you.
chapters: 0:00 Four servers at night, forty at lunch. Who decides, and when?

videos.title: Why Cache and Where: Hit Ratio, Cache Layers & What Not to Cache
videos.summary: Every product page runs the same database query thousands of times a second for data that changes once a day. What if most of those requests never reached the database? That's what a cache does.
chapters: 0:00 The same query runs thousands of times a second. Why ask the database every time?
0:14 The same query, thousands of times

videos.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading): Reads, Writes & Why Delete on Write
videos.summary: You added Redis next to your database. Who fills the cache, when, and what happens when data changes? The most common answer is cache-aside, also called lazy loading.
chapters: 0:00 Who puts data into the cache: your code, or the cache itself?

videos.title: Read-Through vs Write-Through Caching (vs Cache-Aside, DAX)
videos.summary: With cache-aside, every service repeats the same code: check the cache, query the database, fill the cache. What if the cache did that work itself? That's read-through and write-through caching.
chapters: 0:00 Ten services, ten copies of the same caching code. Is there a better way?
2:03 Example: DAX in front of DynamoDB

videos.title: Write-Behind vs Write-Around Caching: Speed vs Durability
videos.summary: A viral video gets 50,000 views a second and every view is a database write. Does each one really need its own write right now? Two patterns answer that: write-behind and write-around.
chapters: 0:00 Fifty thousand tiny writes a second. Can the database keep up?

videos.title: Cache TTL & Expiration: How to Choose a TTL and Why Add Jitter
videos.summary: Cache prices for an hour and customers see stale sale prices; cache for a second and the cache barely helps. How long should data live in a cache, and why do smart teams add randomness to that number?
chapters: 0:00 How long should cached data live: a second, an hour, forever?

videos.title: LRU Cache Explained: O(1) Hash Map + Doubly Linked List (Python)
videos.summary: The cache is full and one more entry arrives. Which one goes? The most common answer, in interviews and in production, is the least recently used one. Here's how LRU works and how to build it in O(1).
chapters: 0:00 The cache is full. Which entry should go?

videos.title: LFU vs LRU vs FIFO Cache Eviction (and TinyLFU) Explained
videos.summary: A nightly scan touches a million old products once each, and an LRU cache throws out your best-sellers to make room. Recency alone was fooled. Let's look at LFU, FIFO and modern TinyLFU.
chapters: 0:00 One big scan wipes your whole cache. How?
